At close of this sweet spring-time day, • I roam through flower-clad fields, Bright hues, sweet scents of pleasant May. Each mead ard hedge-row yields. And see, this grass-grown path beside. A bunch of cowslips flung, Whose yellow clusters late, in pride O'er humbler daisies hung. Gathered but fent' short hours bygone. Why do they wither here, . • Beheld by few, bewailed bv none, On this hedge-shaded bier • Enase child, perchance, wearied with play, Or lured by objects new. Thase once prized treasures cast away, To fade in night's cold dew. -chance some love-sick iillage laci gad given them to his lass, And she, or jealous, ve,xed, or sad, Had tossed them on the grass. Maply_sorne man, care-worn or old, Remembering childhood's house. Dr lamed he might wake hopes dead and cold, By grasping childhood's flowers: ix AaJttl.:l Allen found the old-time fragrance fled mutt made them once so sweet, 'Flung them abide, and onward sped . . • With sorrow-laden feet. Mayhap a mother, whose loved child. , Such gathered e'er he died, For his. sake plucked these flow'rets wild, • Dropped whilst she wept and sighed. . . But who may guess why these were torts From pastures where they pew? . , Enough, they for this fate were born, , And fed by sun and dew. For him who writes, for him who reads, What holdeth fate in store? To be cast forth as worthless weeds, Or grow from' less to more? Freston, May, 1881. D.

IH MILK SETTING.—PSOUSSOr Arnold gays, in the Tribune, in answer to an irileirer :—Among the many exeelleet modes for raising cream, I would not like to KW which ia hest, if indeed any one is best under all circum- stances. It will suffice to state a few general principles, mei let etch One decide for himself. 1. To make the Airiest flavoureel and longest k,eeging,betthr the cream must undergo a ripeniriii process by exp6sure to the oxygen of the air while it is sweet. This is hest done while it is rising. The ripening is very tardy. when the 'temperature is low. 2. After cream becornes soar', the; more`liperiing the more it depreciates. The sooner it is then skimmed and churned the better, hat i should nofbe churned while too new. The best time for skimming and churning is just before acidity becomes apparent. 3.-Cream wakes better hurter toerise in cold air than to rim in cold water, but it will rise sooner in cold water, mid the milk will keep sweeter 'longer:: 4: The deeper milk' i iet; -the leter airing the &kiln gets while rising. 5. The depth of Setting should vary with the tem- perature; the lower it is, the deeper milk' may be set; the higher, the shallower it should be. Milk should never he set eha low in a low temperature, nor deep In a high one. Setting deep in cold water econcimises time, labour, arid space. 6. "While:milk' ie standing for cream to rise the purity of the creams and consequently 'the fine flavour and keeping of the butter, will be injured if the. surface of the cream is exposed freely to air much warmer than the cream. •7. When cream is colder than the surrounding air, it takes up moisture and impurities ham the air„ When the air is colder than the Cream, it takes up moisture and whatever escapee from the cream. In the former case the cream puri- fies, the surrounding ;in the latter, the air helps to purify the cream The selection of a creamer should hinge on what is most desired—highest quality, or greatest con- venience aid economy in time, space, and labour. • ---: A large meeting of cnemployed la.bourers was held me Saturday at Harold's Cross, Dublin. Black banners were displayed, and the speakers declared that labourers could not endure their present condition much longer. After the meeting a serious ercounter with the police took place, IR which several constables were severely hurt. Three of the rioters, named Kelly, Macdonald, and Lennon were arrested, anti in the evening were sentenced to six months' imprison- ment. An agrarian murder of an exceptionally cruel character has been committed near Athenry, in county Galway. The victim was a fa, mer named Dempsey, who occup'ed SOMe land from which a former bolder had been evicted. His ini-• mediate predecessor on the farm, one Marty Hynes, SUr. rendered the property at the instance of the Land Leagues and for so doing he figures as the hero in ballads which are sung in the district. Dempsey's defiance of the "unwritten law, marked him out for punishment, and be met his fate in the saddest of circu hstances. He was going to mass OIS Sunday forenoon, when, from behind a wall, his assassin., shot him in the back, and his death was witnessed by his tie° children, who were accompanying him to divine services Iwo men have been arrested on suspicion. . Sareeral coats had been stnlen.—Mr. George Moss, who .managed the business on behalf of Mr. Walker, identified one of 'the coats pro- dnced as his property.—A canal censtable named George Weedall stated that early on the previous Thursday more- leg be heard a disturbance on hoard a schooner in the Fen- • ton dock, and some one who pointed to the prisoner said, " Thar,. tie fellow that ate my dinner." He mdered him away. The ittendalice officer of the Runcorn School Board (Mr. Bowyer) has had a complaint lodged against him by Mr. Annett, the master of Trinity Church schools, to the effect that be has taken upon himself to recommend a scholar belongingr to that school to attend Halton school. Mr. Bowyer laid before the BOW d at their meeting on Wednesday, a letter statin.{ that for the future Mr. Arlinet should decline to give him any more returns. The matter was fully investigated by the members. Mr. Lea did hi a best to defend the action of Mr. Annett, but Mr. Bowyer was strongly supported by Mr. John Simpson and Mr. Nor- man. The conduct of tke 'Link), schoolmaster w,s most strongly, condemned, on the ground that Mr. Bowyer had always been found to discharge his duties with the most perfect impartiality, and he denied that there wai. the slightest truth in the statement of hie eminent. Accord- ing to Mr. Simpson's account, the attendance officer is general favourite with the teachers at the Wesleyan school, and that gentleman expressed his surprise that though Mr Bowyer was apparently very well liked by the teachers of the town generally, he appeared to b quite unable to platter the master of Trinity. As far as lam able to judge without hearing what Mr. Annett I as to sty, he app..ars to have acted with a want of tact in attacking the attendance officer, who is generally liked. as the discussion caused certain reports to conic to the surface, the circulation of which cannot do any good. The master of Trinity school was formerly at Widnes. and the Rev. W. Preston, vicar of Holy Trinity. paid a very high catnpliment to him at a meeting of Churchmen hell at that town some short time ago. It may be as well that the public should reserve their decision ,on the subject until they have heard what Mr. Annett Iles to say in defence. The time is very rapidly approaching when the chairman of the Runcorn Board of Commiseioners will be appointea for the official year. I should magine that Mr. Philip Speakman ought to stand a good chance of election after the many years he had been on the Board. There is some talk of appointing Dr. Steele, but I cannot forget the saying of the late Premier that the unexpected always happens, and some outsiders may, after all, win the race. The late action of Mr. Dolby, the Government auditor, in surcharging several members of the Runcorn Board of Com- missioners so heavily, and in 'regard to particulars which ha has quietly passed in previous years, has caused much adverse comment in Rgincorn. SITDDRN DRAM 07 • GIRL AT Sr. HELENS.—A girl named Blidget Doyle, 16 years of age, who resided with ber parents at 71, Union-street, died suddenly in the shop of James G.trner, College-street, en Tfiesday. Deceased had Always been a weak girl, and latterly had been subject to tits. On Tuesday her mother sent her for tobacco to Mr. Garner's, and while waiting she said, "I have such a had pain in my head; I an fainting."' Water was given to her, hut she grew worse, and died in the shop in the presence of several persons. Flom. Cuoss BAZAAR, Sr. HELINS.—The results of this bazaar amounts to about £B3O. This result, which has so agreeably surprised the promoters, is due to the efforts, admirable alike, in their generosity and unanitnity of the town. The pming was a failure, mainly, no doubt) owing to their 'neap., i:nce. The wealthier friends, expected on the first day, for the most part excused themselves at the last moment. It is a fact, that for the first three hours the impression was ithsheatrtening one; but from that time the success was unva,ying, a result due to the kindness and hearty co-operation of .a large number of our Protestant fellow townspeople, as well as to the universal generosity of the Cathodes, not of this district only, hut of the whole of Sr. Helens. The Fathers desire us to be the means of com- municating to the public the very great gratitude which they feel towards their numerous benefactms. KsfllaE rITAMEIRR Or COICKESCE. • -The members of the Cheshire Chamber of Agriculture held their half. yearly meeting at Crewe, on Thursday; Mr. G. W. Latham presiding. The report of the Council spoke in con- gratulatory terms of the improved harvest prospects, owing to the recent spell of good weather. The winter was very, severe, and cold easterly winds of the spring were pro- tracted into the middle of May ; but their effect on arable land had been good, and the grass lands, though late, were fast filling up both in meadow and pastures, while grain and green crops gave promise of a good harvest. Dairy stocks were healthy, and free from pleuro-pneumonia and foot-and- mouth disease.

A RAINAILL HAY LAD STRAW D.'ALER IN TROUBLE. At the Baenett-street police court, Liverpool, on Saturday John Richardson, described as a hay and straw dealer residing at Rainhill, WM charged on remand with obtaining a load of straw of toe value of £4 13a. 5d., under false pre- tences. from Mr. Mark Wright, Gill Moss Farm, West Derby. From the evid.nce of the prosecutor, it appeared that on Wednesday, the 11,h instant, the defendant went to the residence of the prosecutor and ordered a load of straw. which he said he want,d for a Mr. T. A. Wood, cotton broker, of Pilch-lase, Knotty Ash. The straw was forwarded on the following ii .y. hut Mr. Wright dincovered that there was no person of the name of Wood living at Knotty Ash. Prosecutor admitted that defendant had offered him the money for the straw, bid he refused to accept it, as he had then put the matter in the hands of the police. Defendant denied any intention of stealing the straw, and further ohaerved that it was a custom amongst dealers to purchase straw in other people's name's, became if the seller knew he was selling it to a dealer he would raise the price. Defendant was committed for trial, bait being accepted. 1 DASTARDLY ATV. Descending front his engine, he soon showed that there was god cause fir the stoppage by producing from before the engine wheels an iron "choir." which had been placed upon the rail by some evil-disposed persona or persons with an evident intention to upset the train, Though not " keyed " uplt the rail, the" chair " was, in a clumsy manner hetokaniflr. haate, secured—it is maid with a string. SEMEN DRAM AT St HattmeS.—Auti Robinson, 3, Randon-street, 51 years of age, died suddenly at noon n Monday. Deceased was the wife of James Robinson, a labourer, and had enjoyed good health. About eight o'clock in the Morning while in the kitchen she complained of pains in her stomach, and was unable to partake of any breakfast. With the assistance of her husband she undressed here,' f and got into bed. Becoming worse her husband saw Dr. Griffiths, whe gave him some medicine and pills, some of which were administered to deceased. She continued to grow worse, and died about twelve o'clock. Dr. Griffiths stated the probable cause of death was apoplexy. MYSTERIOUS Drxrii IN A. Lonorno-Flotres.—Under peculiar ci rcumetances, a man totally unknown was found dead in bed at the lo.l4ing-honse, of Elizabeth Lee, roan Hill, Warrington, on Monday morning. Deceased, who had the appearance of an Irish labourer, and was about 60 years of age, obtained lodginge at Mrs. Lee's on Saturday night. On Sunday he complained of having a severe cold, and he only once during that day tat. d food. He slept with a mut named Marsh, who arose the morning following about Riven o'clock, hut did net mike anything wrong with de- ceased. During the forenoon another lodger entered the room amid seeing that deceased was laid very still, went to the bedside, and discovered that he was dead. There were no marks of. any description on the deceased. On Wednes- day Mr. C. E. county coroner, held an inquest on the body at the Griffin Inn. No light was thrown upon the i tentity of the deceased, am.t a verdict of " Death from natural causes" was returned.

THE BOATING ACCIDENT AT WARRINGTON.

Sir,—Generally speaking, after having read the paper regularly for a manner '0 years.'l have found the reports of local events contained in • The Ezaminer to be correct; but I I was somewhat surprised to find in your issue of Saturday., ' • hot, that this rule had been departed- from in your report of . , the boating accident at Warrington: Your correspondent .• ' says, "That the twe young men in endeavouring to • extbaage setts caused til4 boat to list suddenly, tic." The. fact is they had not taken their rests, having been standing, up all the time in pushing the boat off the bank, and when about to twat themselves they overbalanced the boat. Re also say that " the young lady by standing' at one end of the tot was carnptrately dry. and at the solicitation of one of the young men she gallantly mounted his back, but over- come probably by the ludicrousness of the situation, she let - go her hold and slide,' ungracefullyinto the water, and had 7 to wade to the hank with the rest of the party." The fact is that the young lady being sat down at the end of the • beat which tined with water first,- was quite as wet as anv- one else, and as tile water was only about a foot deep to the liver bank there watt. no necessity for her getting on the .• young man's back, and she walked straight out of the boat •! to the bank. as for gallantly mounting the young man's .back, I should fancy your informer only wrote that to see - how ludicrous; it would appear. Trusting your corresnon- *. -dent will havenotnething of [note public- interest to report in future issues than of trying' to make a public laughing Stock, thrOmth incorrect repodink, of two or three persons • .4 who got up to the kneee in the rieer.--I ant, yours truly, o•7' rdeVarriagton, Jane 2nd, 1881: • G. W. correspondent who sepplied the paragraph in question nitrites us flat the facts were cOrrectly reported by hint as ite was an eye witness of tl:e accident.—Entruao] - CRICKET. • , FRODEDIAM 2ND ELNVM (?) v. LAMENTABLE DEATH. • OF A IVAItnINGTON CHEMICAL .MANUFACI'URER. An inanest was held at the Coach and Horses inn, War- rington, on Motday, orr the body of Mr. William Long- shaw, jun., chemical manufacturer, Sankey Bridges, who, • died on Satnrciay; tinder very lamentable circumstances, as will be gathered from the evidenc,, which was as follows ' Peter Phillips Long,vhaw, Sycamore Bank. Great .anitey, deposed :—The deceased was my brother, and was 31 years*,, • of age. Ile and myself were 'in business with our father, Mr. William Longehaw, at our chemical manufactory, in I. Little Sankey, both •of us living with, our fatiatr. In the, works deceased had the works department chiefly, and I the ' • business., On Saturday [noshing, the 28th May, shortly • before eleven in the foreniirin I was in the office writing, Mr. Sonter, the clerk, being also present. Deceased came in, but ' • I did not notice him till be called to me—." Peter. I have svralbwed some carbolic in' mistake." He was then stand- • leg at the desk tnd and had already set down the bottle—an old quart charnpagnenpiin thc desk, I jumped up asking • him t° "me with. MP- 'wbicii he did, arid .1 gee him perhaps - bag a --a 01 ef oil, which he drank. I then asked him how he . came to have made such.* mistake. He said that he thought , it was a bottle of herb !seer, and he was sure it was all over with him, as he bad certainly swallowed some. As the trap was slaaAling in tie yard he pn.posed to get to town to see doctor, and he went in:o the office, got his coat, put it on, and then gettl.ng into the trap , with his father and myself, - be himself drove to Warrington. Or the way he consmettml driving furiously, and I. took the reins from his hand, ask- lug him if he felt pain. Is made no reply, but shook his head. On art iring at Mr. Young's, the di•uggist, in Sankey- street, be got down and we went in, deceased staggerieg a little in so doing. There they gave him two or three ounces more oil, advising his being got to a doct^r iminediately. I took him across to Dr, Huson-More'e, And he seeing deceased .tt advised his being got at once to the Infirmary. His father I and myself got him in the trap again driving Ulnae direet 'IO" to the Infirmary. Ha seemed fast failing, and I supported k him with one arm and drove at the same time. We lifted • *him down and carried him, but lie was dying, and expired L' In a few minute. The doctor and Dr. Pox both SAW de- b: :"ceased, but nothing could be done for him, I believe. He had not spoken since we got into' town. He did not appear- to be in much pain so far as! could Wise.. Hat was in capital health previously, and up to this happening. Nothing • was then wrong with hitn.—indeed, be seemed brighter it, anything, than common. The bottle in question had been. received that morning from Birmingham as it sample, " and was, • unfortunately, wholly without label, the. cork too being left partially nut instead of being • • driven right up as usual. In the summer time we occasionally have herb beer in the office, but have not had any as yet this summer. What deceased may have had himself. I cannot speak to. I believe he las drunk this , staff under the misimpression be mentioned. I had been speaking with him sbortiv before, and be was quite col- lected and comfortable in his mind. 'There was no neces- °-• sity for the sample 'coming forward, but to save any possibility of dispute, M. Harvey said, "You had better take this ilattle with yon." I said I did not like to carry it in train, and he said he vrosiktuend it, and it got there about ten o'clock. I have never seen a bottle came from this firm , without a large lab-1 on the front describing its contents, and the cork cat off level with the top of the bottle. It is very difficult for any One working in carbolic to smell it. Replying te the foreman, witness said :—Deceased was • not at all. depressed. My father only remarked that • morning be was in better spirits that morning than •he had seen . him lately. There was nothing to Mgr. him to be low spirited. In answer to the Corimer., he add:—!! he had wanted a poison he could have gone downstairs and cot 20 poisons which he would have preferred to this. It is a moot distressing thing for anybody to take. Ile hal been a teetotaller for a long time. Miss Helen Hell, nurse at the Infirmary, said: I was presetat on the deceased being brought in, about 11-15 on Saturday morning. He was dying, and expired in only about five minutes aflee coming in. I understood that deceased hail &rink some carbolic by mistake. Ina% Rich- mond had seen him, as Dr. Fox did also, immediately after death, and they expressed no doubt as to this being the cause of death. Joseph Sonter, 31, Aikin-street, clerk to Messrs. Long- • shaw. said he was present in the office when deceased came in. He said, "Oh, Peter, I have drank some carbolic." lie then went downstairs as fast as he could to get tome oil. Deceased said he thought it Was heti) beer. ' He heard him say that diatinctly, ' and he spoke seriously. The oil WAS given to him, aod he saw de- •ceased, Ids brother,' and father get into the trap, and drite off. He afterwards heard of his . death. The boy In the Milne unpacked the bottle. Deceased did not know what-the bottle contained, as he was rot aware •- that it was the bottle taken oat of the bias. With being in the works they coal not sitiell carbolic acid. He had not • the least doubt as to deceased being in sound mind when he did it. It had been done oy mistake, not intentionally. A Juryman : I think, myself, the mistake watt in the bottle being without a label. Witness : The bottle ovine in a box, and he himself told the boy to get the bottle out. By the Coroner They sometimes had drink. They had had a bottle or two this suanner, and he had seen the de- ceased drink from them. They hid herb beer in the bottle similar to that which contained the carbolic acid. The Coroner remarked that the circumstances of the caws were very peculiar. Toe bottle ought only to be in the bands of those who opened it, and they knew perfectly well what they were opening. It had ben given .to Mr. Peter Lengshavr the day before to bring away with him, hut as he explained he did not care to Carr/ i', and he' 1.11 it !loan to send on. THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY JUNE 4, 1881.

The Anchor steamer M tcedonia ftoin New York for (Hasg,,w went ashore in a fog on Monday on the Scotch coast, and it is feared she Will become a wreck. She carries no passengers. The mutilated body of Mr. John Critchley, a gentleman of good social position in the town, has been found on the doorstep of a house at Batley. Mr. Critchley had been missing for a month. Where he had met his death is a mystery. It was not where his body was found, for decom- po•tition had commenced. At the Eckington petty sessions. James Reaney, of Dronfielti, and Robert Atkin, labourer, were remanded on the charge of attempting to blow up the boilers at 4eBBlB Stainforth's sickle works, Hackenthorpe, by placing in them a quantity of gunpowder and a fuse. The prisoners said they were engaged to do the job for £l5 by a third man. who had escaped.

- _ THE LAW As TO AFFILIATION ORDERS.-. 411 the Queen's Bench Division, on Monday,' before , Baron Huddleston and Mr. Justice Hawkins, in Hardy V, Atherton, Mr. M'Clyment appeared for the appellant, Hannah Hardy;and Mr. Croome for the respondent, William Atherton. It wasan appeal on a special case from a declaim of the LancaShire justices; at Newton refusing to continues bastardy order on the ground that the wolean having married, her. 'husband was in a position to maintain the child. The respondent, it was stated, was,the.putative father of a child born Of; the, appellant on the' 9th May, 1877: She Was then a single woman, and in' the month of August following else aptilied to the justices atNeistad for an order.upen the defendant, which was granted, to roay 55.. per Week. until the child had attained the age of 19 years. Her maiden nanie was Hannah Verder. In March, IfiBo she married James Hardy, and the respondent was thereupon advised that he order of the jus- tices was Suspended durirt,g the exiiience of the Marriage inasmuch as there could not be a thieble'penalty for the maintenance of the child. In giving Judgment, Baron Hud- dlestan said it was obvious from the Acts Mitring upon this subject, that the Legislature did not intend that the order in such cases should cease to have operation on the marriage of the mother. The putative father Was bound to pay for the maintenance of the child so long as the moHter lived and *aid sound mind until the child had attained a certain 'age. He entertained no doubt, under the circumstances in this case,that the order upon the putative father continued to exist although the mother might have married' and her 'husband be ma a position to maintain it.—Mr. Justice Haw- kine concurred, and, in doing so, said he was fully of opinion that the order'could be forced notwithstanding the fact of the marriage of the appellant and the ability of' her bushand to support and maintain the chill. Common sense and humanity told us that the putative father ought not to be relieved from contributing to his offspring. He (Mr. Justice Hawkins) rejoiced to think that since the days of that chaste, virtuous, and humane sovereign, Elizabeth. oar laws had been so humanised. so to speak, that a bastard child had ' no longer to be shunned as a thing whose legitimate posi- tion was that of a pauper, and whose legitimate house was the workhouse. Even an illegitimate child by the humanity of the law might now find itself a member of an honest family, and the sole obligation cast upon its parent was that , be might be compelled to bear his fair and proper share to its maintenance.—Mr. Croome rose to ask for leave to ap- wal, but their Lerdships refused the application.—Mr. Justice Hawkins said that the armel'ant must have her co4s.—The appeal was therefore allowed, with costs. NEWTON PET mr Bassiows.—At these sessions, on Satur- day, before Messrs. Birley. Comber, and Houghton, James Newsham, charged with keeping a dog without a license, on the 3rd ult.; was fined 10s. and costs.--Samuel Wilcock, for using threatening langua .13 towards one Harriet Littler, was bound over to keep the peace for six months in the sum of IVO and two sureties in £s,—Helen True was summoned for

using language calculated to create a breach of the peace towards a neighbour named Alice Wilcock; and Elizabeth Lee was charged with ill-treating and assaulting Alice. Wilcock. This was a neighbour's quarrel, and the magis- trates bound the three women over to keep the peace for six months.—Jonathan Turton was charged with threatening to _ . . .

assault one James Budworth, and also doing damage to a fence belonging to the complainant .to, the extent of ss. Complainant, who is the occupier of a small farm at Gol- borne, had frequently to complain of the damage done to his fields by the hens of the defendant trepassing upon his land. He had frequently spoken to defendant about the eratter, but he did not listen to hini: On the 25th ult. a number of defendant's hens were upon complainant's land, and he en- deavoured to turn them off and fired it gun over the heads of two of them. Defendant appeared to have becotne ex- asperated at this, and threatened to assault the complainant and his son. He also began to pull up a fence which be- longed to complainant, and did damage to the extent named. The Bench hound defendant over in £lO to keep the peace for six months, and ordered him to pay the damage done to the fence.—John Brannen was Lharged with being drunk at GoThorne, on the 12th March; and further with being drunk at Golhorne Railway Station and assault- ing the police on the 21st May. P.C. 81 said be was assaulted by the defendant when be took him into custody let the railway station on the day in question. Defendant was drunk and resisted -eery much, Defendant was fined Sc. and costs for being drunk in the first case, 10s. and' costs I in the second, and was committed, for three months' lin- prisenment for ' assaulting the poliee.—George Cook, labourer, was charged with stealing a duck, value 35., the t,roperly of JAlnz Fox, the landlord of the Victoria Inn, Wargrave. The complainant . said he kept a number, of ducks. He missed one of them on Thursday last, but it was tifterwards found concealed in a haystack in the yard. HE obtained a constable, who on going to look for 'the duck some time after prisoner had been seen about found it was taken away. The officer went to the prisoner's house anti ' found the duck concealed under the seat of a sofa. Pi isoner , was committed to gaol for 14 days.

TIOWTER presented his returns from the public ele- mentary schools for May. as followed :—Certified Govern- ment accommodation, 2,289 ; total number on the rolls, 2 792 ; tot it average attendance, 1,938 8 : average atten- lance V.,. These figures show an increase in the average attendance as compared with the corresponding period of las year of 1688, and an increase as compared with 1874, the year preceding the formation of the Board, of 70614. The 'otal somber in attendance at private adventure schools under 9.1. per week was 56. During the past month he had dealt w;th the remaining cases ordered to be summoned for contravention of the bye-laws. The total number of persons summon, dto apnear before the magistrates was 27. Con- victions were granted in 26 eases, and the usual fine of 6d and 4s. 64. costs imposed. The other case was dismissed, there being a doubt shout the youth's correct age. The proceedings then terminated.

The INSPECTOR: Ills only fair that land in the immediate neighbourhood of any sanitary improvement should pay its fair share of rates. What do the ratepayers in Frodshatn township think about the matter? Several Voices: They don't care much about it either way. (Laughter.) The proposed boundary as affecting Runcorn mud Halton were next considered. The gentlemen present from Runcorn were the Rev. Canon Barclay, Messrs. William Handley, William Whittaker (overseer.). William Sutton (assistant overseer), P. Briscoe, Dr.McD nigall, Thomas Rimy, Tames Pritchard, and M. Ba, ker (aarveyor). Mr. HANPLEY gave a uutal.er of explanations to the Inspector, iq elucidation of the different boundaries pro- posed, and in favour of the one adopted by the com- missioners' meeting and the one composed of ratepayers. Dr. MoDomattr, delivered a long speech, which was a repitition of the arguments advanced by him at the rate- payers meeting against the iniquitous change which would he brought about if the boundary proposed by the guardians were adopted. The INSPECTOR interrupted the doctor, telling him that what be %canter: was not a speech, but evidence. MnDounaat: Quite true. Mr. Ttromas Wiatotar, of Halton, was against the boundary suggested by the comtnissioners, as it would cause the Halton people to have to pay to the Runcorn School Board rate, and they had net long since gone to an expense of £5OO in enlarging the grammar school. The INSPECTOR said that the alteration of the boundary would not necessarily cause Halton to be included in the Runcorn School Board district. Mr. HENRY LTNAICER objected to the boundary sub- mitted to the Local Government Board being called the guardians' boundary, as they did not care three straws how lehe hounilary was tixed. 'IATNAKER, an clerk to the cdinmissioners' gave a full description of the reasons why the members of that body were in favour of the boundary adonted at their meeting, which was the sante as the one approved at the ratepayers' meeting. Mr. BESWICK, agent to the Marquis of Choltnondley, who 1 has property in Halton and Runcorn, said the boundary suggested by the commissioners would meet his employer's views very well. Mr. ROBERT HOLLAND, on behalf of Sir Richard Bronke, Bart., opposed the botrudary of the guardians on the ground that it put in a number of farmhouses in HAltom and managed to leave out a great amount of land. If the com- missioners would agree to leave the farmhouses referred to in Halton, the boundary (with this alteration) would suit Sir Richard very well. After an adjournment for luncheon, the Inspector took evidence as to the townships of Antroban., Sevenoaks, Norley, Crowton, and Kingsley. In the case of each of these there was no opposition. Th, hisraarota said he would report to the Local Go- vernment Board, and their decision would be made known in due course. We may add that Mr. Dansey cnnilucted the enquiry with very great ability, anti raised none of 'those wearying quibbles by which some inspectors from the Local Gavern- ment Board ofliee manage to occupy houra of valuable time. We heard enconiama pronounced up in hint from gentle- men representing all sides of the question under considera- 'ion.

TUE REV. JOLIN YON(E ON THE REVISE!) NEW TESTAMENT. On Sunday morning an eloquent discourse on the above subject was delivered in Wycliffe Congregational Church by the Rev. John Yonge to a large congregation. The rev. gentleman took for his text 2 Peter i., 19, "We have the word of prophecy made more sure; whereuam ye do well that ye take heed." Revised version. In the old version it read thus, "We have also a more sure word of prophecy," &a. He said: This text, as it stands in the revised version, bears very apt reference, by accom;nodation, to that version itself. In a very striking sense the revised version of Ve New Testa- ment is the Christian's " word of pronheey made more sure." It can hardly he disputed that never before has the world possessed so accurate a rendering of the New Testa- ment; Fe accuracy is abundantly assured by the mani- fold sources of information as to the original text that are now accessible, by the unquestioned learning of the large companies of English and American scholars who have done the work, and also by the deliberate and painstaking ewe with which the work has beer ddne. We may take this re- vised version in hand, at least then with this assurance,— that in whatsoever else it may justly awaken diyergdrice of opinion, it lays indisputable claim to as nearly absolute an accuracy as can be realised. It is, indeed, in this sense "the word of prophecy made more sure." 'lt has been well pointed out by many of the speakers and writers who have already found utterance Upon tide subject, that no greater event has happened in to- cent days than the issue of this Revised New Testament. Many events have made more noise, and created more stir. But, few events, if any, are likely to have a deeper, or more abiding. far-reaching result than the issue of this book. By I nothing which has happened in our day at least, has there been given so wide a stimulus to the reading of the New Testament as is given to it by this event. The attention of vast multitudes will be turned anew to the Gospels and the Enisties, in rhanv cases no doubt simnly from curiosity, to discover wherein the new version differs from the old, but in many cases also to discover what new light has been cast upon the doctrines aqd facts of the Christian religion. The effect upon men of this renewed contemplation of the New Testament cannot be other than healthful. We may go further, and believe, that as the word of God is powerful to human salvation, many souls will be brought "from dark- ness to light, and from the power of satan unto God" by the 11 issue of this book. This event is destined to accomplish a quiet, but real evangelisation. Curiosity may do for maui- tauten of the readers of this new version as gaol a work as it did for Zacchams ; it may bring them within a sight of Christ, and they may have eceSSion lo say that the day wherein they took home a copy of the Revised Version, was the day when, so far as they were concerned, "salvation came to their house." It is difficult to think about this quiet and unosten- tatious but unspeakably significant event without being most profoundly moved by it. A new distribution of the gospel of salvation, which, in less thana fortnight, is b 4 be counted by millions of copies, eagerly caught up in this country and America, is a fact which means far more than we Can say. It means, at least, that interest in the Bible is very wide- spread and very real. It shows that men are intent upon gaining all the light they can upon the facts and teachings of scripture. It suggests that the Bible has made a place for itself in human esteem which neither time and c'dange nor error and unbelief can destroy. And there is no token in the eagerness with which men in this country and America are possessing themselves of this revision, that the world, oven its educated and cul- tured classes, has voted the Bible obsolete. Even newspapers pause to write eloquent articles upon the event, and upon the hook; and it is almost a surprise to find feorn the language of some of them how deeply intense is the popular veneration for scripture. The fact, however, that the newspaper press finds it worth while to occupy so much space upon this mat- ter, is a sign that the Bible is held dear by the great mass of the English people. We may rejoice to recognise the sign. And inasmuch as this new version is purged from misleading and erroneous renderings of the words of Christ and His apostles, while it also con- firms with greater emphasis and accuracy the doctrines commonly received as Christian, it cannot be other than that this issue will exercise incalculable influence for good upon mankind. There is a manifest divineness about the whole event. God is again speaking, as with new voice, to the world; and though he is doing so with the quiet still. nose of a printed book, it will be found that even these days of sensation and excitement and noise, can respond with worshipful faith to this "still small voice" of the Lord. I. deems to me, therefore, that, as Christians, ws may hail till. event both with gratitude and with high and holy hop. The time at disposal ia this service will not admit of a• much being said as it would be useful to say touch tog this revised versien. In pe.sing, however, i seems fitting to say this—that in a church hear ing the honoured name of Wycliffe. a heart, ,eception may properly be given to this new English versie' of the Testament. Wycliffe's great and immortal di, tinction is that he largely, if not entirely, contributed wards placing the Scriptures, for the first time, is the hands

THURSDAY.—Before Mr. Holbrook tiaskell, June. A WARRINGTON DEALER'S ADVENTURE WITH A WIDNES Winow.—Sarah Thornten and Ann Gordon were charged with stealing £lO in gold from the person of Wm. Plinston, general dealer, 22, Catherine-streer, Warrington.—Tbe Inspector of Police said that on Tuesday prosecutor attended a sale in Church-street, and bought a table. While at the sale he saw Thornton, who got into conversation with him about the table. She afterwards told him that she was a widow, and lived at 51, Church-street, where she would be glad to see him at any time. Nothing further took place at that time, hut he sold the table to somebody in Church- street, and on Wednesday came for the money. After transacting the business he went into the Bridge Inn, where he had five or six glasses of beer and remained there until 7 or Bin the evening. He then went to the prisoner Thor,. ten's house. On her openang the door she said she was very glad to see him, and invited him inside. He complied wit), her invitation and sat on the sofa. In a short time he fell asleep. Previously to his going into the house he counted his money and placed it in a bag and put it in his trousers pocket. There was £l4 10s. in gold. He awoke Rhea 12 o'clock and found that the purse was part out of his pocket, and on examining it found that £lO had been abstracted. He charged Thornton with stealing it, and told her if she did not give it up he would inform the police. The prisoner Gordon was then in the house with a man named Foley, and another man was just outside the door. Gordon took up the poker and said she would strike him. She also said that neither she nor her sister had taken the money. Foley also add hewould put him out if he did not mind what he was saying. He thought he was the master of the house. He then went and told the police. The police had searched for the money, but had been unable to find it. He therefore asked for a remand until the c tse could be properly coin- nleted. The two men who were at the house had satisfac- torily accounted for their presence, and no charge would he brought against them. Gordon was the sister of Thornton, and a married woman,—Prosecutor gave evidence in support, of the Inspector's statement, after which the prisoners were remanded until Wednesday next, and bail refused.

The translation of eae New Testament, which appeared in the version Of the esaae knewit as Wvcl e 5 is believed to have been almost exclusively Wycliffe's personal work It would, therefore, he a somewhat serione neglect and incen,iwency if we— who glory in his name—were slow or indifferent in our re- ception of this latest development of the wotk he eo nobly commenced. How wenderfully times have changed since his day ! Then, such an attempt as his was only accom- plished in the teeth of much oppremition and even persecu- tion. Men said then "It is heresy to speak of Holy Scripture in English." Wycliffe's enemies called his work of transl ttin "a daring impit tv " ; and Patliatnent was moved to order thst all epics of the Scripture should he seiz id and destroyed. We cannot forget, either, that in the course of English history, men have lost their lives in the work of Bible tranelation ; and the work recently done so peacefully by owe Revision Canimittee has earned for men in the pest the martyr's crown Verily, times have changed! We believe that the translated Bine, becoming the birth- rieht, of every Englishman, has, under God, worked the change. I can fancy, however, that some people may be asking in a good deal of perplexity, o What need is there for a revision ! What is the matter with our grand old Bible? Have we been pinning our faith to a book full of mistakes ?" Quite prob obl• ; also, some will be in no little dismay about the ultimate effect of this revised version, as, indeed, certain dienitnries of the Church of England have shewn themselves to be already. The fear may arise in ROMs minds whether the resettled version may not strike at the root of some widely received doctrines, and whether, consequently, it can he safe to accept it. In reference to this kind of feeling, let me say on the one hand that there is need ref a revision of scripture, and on the ether that so far at least as this version of the New Testament is con- cerned, we have no cause to be afraid of it. The revision his reversed none of the generally aecepted doctrines of the hristian faith. It has not revealed any substantial error in our Christian creed. Although, if it ha t —if this learned and careful revision of the Testament, made, as it has been merle, from the original Greek of the oldest and most authentic manuscripts of the sacred writings—if it had altered any doctrine hitherto believed—as lovers of truth. early one course would have been open to us. Our object is to arrive at truth. We believe that the truth of God was con- veyed supremely to the world hy Jesus Christ, and by the A poetlee whom tie commiseioned. We want to know, there- fore. really and absolutely, what Christ and His Apostles did Rey, end do, and teach. And hence, if in our old version doctrinal errors had crept in, it would be te our ieterest to have them found out. When so discovered we should be bound to discard them, because we pin our faith alone to "The truth as it is in Jesus." We need never feer an honest and learned revisinn, which has fir its sole aim accuracy and truth. And so far as this revised Testament is cormerned, we may accept it without distrust, as it leaves our cherished beliefs not only unshaken, but ahundently confirmed. Haying said this, let me now try to explain, so that all may underetand, how it comes to be desirable and needful that our Bible snonid be revised Every one must he familiar with the fact, first of all, that the books of the Bible were written by their authors in Hebrew or Greek ; the Old Testament in the former, the New Testament in the latter language. Our version, therefore, is a translation from those two languages. Moreover, this translation has not been made from printed sources, but from a compariscin of various very ancient manuscripts, which are copies of the books originally written by the several authors. Th 3 original docurnents, it is presumed, have perished. Copies only, at least up to the present day, have been discovered. These copies vary from one another, throveh the accident of incorrect copying, and from other similar accidental reasons. The object of scholara has been for centuries past to compare all the manuscripts that could be discovered, and as the result of such a comparison to frame such a Greek version as might safely become the fount from which to produce an English translation. The version which we have hitherto had in use was produced in some such way as this 270 years ago, in 1611. Now let it he understood that that version was it- self a revision: and the last of a toter rbly numerous series. I 'Phis series of revisione followed, at yeriotts intereals, the first English Bible, which we owe to John Wycliffe. His' Bible wife issued about the year 1382. The earliest revision of that Bible appeared in the short period of six years,— being the revision known as Purvey's, published in 1388. Next after that—in 1535,—nearly 200 years later, came ICoverriale's, speedily followed in 1539 by a version known I as" The great B hie," In 1560 was issued the" Genevan" I version of our English Bible, followed 5 years later by the version known as the Bishop's Bible. Afterwards in 1610 the Dnutti (R. C.) version Was put forth. So that the version of 1611 hitherto in use was really the last of a series of versions, all of them obtained in very similar manner, though with very varying degrees of care and learning. Since 1611 however great changes have taken place in Biblical science, as in all other. Sources of indisputable infer- formation have come to light. Discoveries have been made of manuscripts of the New Testament, either in whole or I I part, of considerahly, older date than any which had been t found prior In 1811. As recently, for example, as 1859, in , the convent of St. Catherine, on Mount Sinai, a intnuscript of the New Testantent was found, which dates hack as early as the 4th century. TEE STATE OF THE HOUSE. • The MASTER reported 477 inmates in the house as against 468 in the corresponding week of last year. During the week 156 t ten, 37 women, and 17 children vagrants had been re- Heys 1. , . , THE VISITING COMMITTEE. The minutes of this committee stated that the committee, having considered the, application of Mr. Mackey for the children to be allowed to visit their parents at the work- house on Sunday afternoons, recommend, that the parents themselves be allowed to visit their children at the schools on the appointed visiting days—viz., the first Friday in each month, from two until four o'clock in the afternoon It was, provided, however, that in cases where the parents were confined to the hospital through sickness their children may visit them at the workhouse during the same intervals. Mr. ..1. R. Mozley reported on the 27th ult. that he had inspected ! the schools, and would report upon them to the Local 1 Government Beard. Thia was all the business of public interest.

The Hull firemen are on strike. About 140 have ceased work, and the nember is increasing as steamers arrive. The present rate of wages is 255. per week for weekly ships, and about £3 ss. per month for steamers running longer pas- s 'gee. The men siy they are, now that trade 'has revived, entitiod io their old rate of wagle,—viz., 28s. weekly boats and £1 monthly, which were reduced owing to depression of trade. Among the unpleasant news from Ireland is a rumour that Lord Duusandle's son was shot dead, on Thureday, near his Loniship's residence in Galway. The report of several policemen hav7ng been killed while assisting at evictions in county Clare is incorrect. There were, how- ever, unlinp,iily, shots fired on both sides, and a telegram from Limerick says that the police killed one man and wounded several others. Twenty of the mob were arrested, all armed with rifles.
